name: Erik Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I write software for delivery depots at a logistics tech firm, about a hundred and twenty people. My part is the picking system, which tells warehouse staff and the little shelf robots which parcel to grab next. A good day is when a depot manager rings to say the morning rush went smoothly. A bad day is a Monday where the scanners in one depot stop talking to our servers and I'm on the phone for six hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, what's going on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancée Sofia, who's a dental hygienist, and we're getting married next September. We put most of our savings into the venue deposit, so right now we've got less than a month of bills in the bank. My pay's below the big-city rate, but there aren't many software jobs here, so I've stayed put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. Probably not far off how it feels some weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but not useless, which is a pretty boring take. At work I'd tell people to keep using it for the dull bits and stop expecting miracles. Online I wouldn't bother saying anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but it doesn't change our money. We've emptied the savings for the wedding, and if my car or Sofia's needs work before September, we're on a credit card. The firm is doing okay, though, because parcels keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI helper for writing test cases now and then, the way I do now. I'd take on the on-call rota for the extra money, two weekends a month. And Sofia and I would set a hard limit on wedding spending, no extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. Money's a bit tight around the edges, but that's the wedding, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine bits might AI still take in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test cases and the release notes, mostly. Maybe the support tickets that just say a scanner is offline. That's an hour a day across the team, so maybe nobody new gets hired, but nobody goes either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first wedding extra you'd drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The band, which hurts because I play bass in a covers band myself. We'd get the lads from my band to play for a few drinks instead. Sofia says that's what she wanted anyway, which I don't fully believe.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped but not useless**, which is a boring take.
I'd tell colleagues to use it for **dull bits** and stop expecting miracles.
think: I'd be relieved, but our **savings** went on the wedding venue deposit.
The firm is **doing okay**, because parcels keep coming whatever happens with AI.
do: Keep using the **AI helper** for test cases now and then.
Join the **on-call rota** two weekends a month for extra money.
Set a **hard limit** on wedding spending with Sofia, with no extras.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a bit **tight** around the edges because of the wedding.
S0.quote: Money's a bit tight around the edges, but that's the wedding, not AI.
fieldNote: His **money pressure** is a chosen one, the wedding, rather than a job threat.
He sees AI taking **an hour a day** across the team and expects fewer hires, not cuts.
He'd swap the paid band for his own **covers band**, which says a lot about him.

steps.text: Keep using the AI helper for test cases now and then
Join the depot on-call rota two weekends a month
Replace the paid wedding band with his own covers band

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. Coding and booking are both in there. That's my whole firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift and companies should be honest about what it means for staff. At work I'd say let's figure out which parts of the picking system AI can actually write. I wouldn't panic in public, because that never helps anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the team shrinks, maybe by a third, and I'm average, so it's a coin toss for me. The thing is, I know the depots. I've stood in the parcel depots at six in the morning watching the shelf robots, and the AI hasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw the senior developers using the new tools for real, I'd learn them properly over a couple of months. I'd ask to move closer to the depots, doing the setup and site visits, because that's the part nobody can do from a screen. And we'd move the wedding to a smaller register office do, keeping some savings back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. It's not doom, but I'd be checking my email for the meeting invite every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sofia say about moving the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say yes faster than I'd like, honestly. Her mum would be the problem. We'd keep the party, just smaller, in her uncle's restaurant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, our newest developer, because new hires are the first to go when work shrinks. She's good, too. I'd try to bring her on the depot visits with me so she learns the side that's harder to replace.

say: I'd say it's a **big shift** and companies should be **honest** with staff.
At work I'd suggest working out which parts of the **picking system** AI can write.
think: The team probably shrinks by **a third**, and I'm average, so it's a **coin toss**.
I know the **depots** in person, at six in the morning, and the AI doesn't.
do: Learn the **new tools** properly once the senior developers use them for real.
Ask to move into **depot setup** and site visits, away from pure screen work.
Swap the big wedding for a **register office** and a smaller party.
feel: **Nervous**, checking for a **meeting invite** every Friday.
S1.quote: I've stood in the parcel depots at six in the morning watching the shelf robots, and the AI hasn't.
fieldNote: He spots his edge in **site knowledge** of the depots, not in code.
He'd shrink the **wedding** fast, showing how money shapes his plans.
Takes junior **Priya** along on visits, a quiet kind of loyalty.

steps.text: Learn the team's AI coding tools over two months
Ask to move into depot setup and site visit work
Swap the wedding venue for a register office and restaurant party

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wow. 2028 is a year and a half after our wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious and the government needs to get people through it, without me pretending I know how. I'd tell friends to keep their heads, pay down debt and not buy houses. I'd probably still avoid posting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the picking software basically writes itself by 2028. My desk job's gone within a year of that. The only thing that buys me time is the depots, because the robots that can do everything people do in there come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd move into whatever depot-side role I could get, even if it pays a bit less, so I'm next to the hands-on work. I'd learn to repair and set up the shelf robots, because someone has to install them until robots can do that too. We'd keep the wedding tiny and put every spare penny into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Not for this year, but for the year after the wedding. Being scared about the year after our wedding is a bad thought to have while you're writing your vows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Sofia's job feel safer than yours here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a few years, yes. You can't do teeth cleaning from a laptop. If my job goes, she'd carry us for a while, which she'd do without a word, and I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2031, when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. Maybe the robot installers are the last ones standing for a bit. I'd be lying if I said I had a plan past that.

say: I'd say it's **serious** and the government must get people through it.
I'd tell friends to **pay down debt** and avoid buying houses.
think: The picking software **writes itself** by 2028, so my desk job goes soon after.
Only the **depots** buy me time, because capable robots don't arrive until around 2031.
do: Take any **depot-side role**, even for slightly less pay, to be near hands-on work.
Learn to **repair and install** the shelf robots before they can do it themselves.
Keep the wedding **tiny** and save every spare penny.
feel: **Scared** about the year **after the wedding**, even while writing his vows.
S2.quote: Being scared about the year after our wedding is a bad thought to have while you're writing your vows.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot gap** by moving to hands-on depot work.
**Sofia's** hands-on job could carry them, which he'd accept but hate.
He has **no plan past 2031** and says so honestly.

steps.text: Move into a depot-side setup role even at lower pay
Train to repair and install shelf-picking robots
Save every spare penny into a joint emergency account
Hold a tiny wedding instead of the booked venue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, five years. That gives me a run-up at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this sensibly, and companies should train their own people instead of firing and rehiring. I'd say it calmly at work, and I'd mean it. I'd vote for whoever has an actual retraining plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I get two or three good years as a developer, then I need to be somewhere else. The depots give me three more years after that, until the robots in 2034. A move to the parcel depots is a plan with an end date, which isn't the same as a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first two years I'd get onto the depot side and take an industrial robotics course the firm part-funds. We'd keep the wedding as planned, just cheaper. I'd aim for three months of savings before I make any move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more in control. Five years feels like enough to make a couple of good decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a plan with an end date. What would you do after it ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd hope by then something new exists that I can't picture yet. Twenty years ago my job didn't exist either. That's not much of a plan, but it's what I believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Sofia change anything about having kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably wait a couple of years more than we planned. I'd want to know I've still got work before there's a baby. Sofia would say I'm overthinking it.

say: I'd say there's time to do this **sensibly**, and firms should **train their own** staff.
I'd vote for whoever has a real **retraining plan**.
think: I get two or three **good years** as a developer, then I need to move.
The depots give three more years, but it's a plan with an **end date**.
do: Move onto the **depot side** within two years.
Take the firm's part-funded **industrial robotics** course.
Save **three months** of bills before making any move.
feel: **Uneasy** but more **in control**, with time for a couple of good decisions.
S3.quote: A move to the parcel depots is a plan with an end date, which isn't the same as a career.
fieldNote: He knows his developer job thins out within a few years, so this is **anxious**.
His plan has a **clear sequence**: depot, robotics course, savings first.
He'd **delay children** a little, a quiet sign of how seriously he takes it.

steps.text: Take the firm's part-funded industrial robotics course
Transfer to a depot-side role within two years
Save three months of bills before any job move
Wait two extra years before trying for a baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable, almost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to adjust if people are sensible, and that schools should start changing now. I'd tell younger friends not to panic and not to ignore it either. That's about as dramatic as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine for the next five or six years as a developer. I'd see the change coming because the senior people would start using new tools before me. After that I'd want to be in the depot or robot side, but there's no rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and learn the new tools when the team does. I'd build savings properly after the wedding, aiming for three months by year three. Around year five I'd start the robotics course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a bit of worry in the background. Ten years of warning is something to plan for, not something to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's my risk exactly, because I wait for others. But I'd be in the depots every month for work, so I'd see the new robots before most people. I trust that to wake me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change for the wedding or kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd go ahead as planned, and probably have a kid in a few years. Ten years is too long to wait on anything.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough if people are sensible, and schools should **change now**.
I'd tell younger friends **not to panic** and not to ignore it either.
think: I'd be fine as a developer for the next **five or six years**.
After that I'd want to be on the **depot or robot side**, but there's no rush.
do: Learn the **new tools** when the rest of the team does.
Build **three months** of savings by year three, after the wedding.
Start the **robotics course** around year five.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a bit of **background worry**.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is something to plan for, not something to lose sleep over.
fieldNote: His **own job** feels safe for years, so the mood is uneasy rather than anxious.
He relies on **depot visits** to warn him in time, a practical early-warning signal.
**Family plans** go ahead unchanged with a decade's notice.

steps.text: Learn the new coding tools alongside the rest of the team
Save three months of bills by the third year
Start the industrial robotics course around year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right after the wedding, when we'd have nothing saved. What would help is firms having to retrain their own staff before cutting them, and a short course in robot installation that's free for people like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the people in the depots think. Everyone talks about developers, but the parcel pickers on the early shift will meet AI before I do. They should be in this study too.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about developers, but the parcel pickers on the early shift will meet AI before I do.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old** developer writing picking software for parcel depots.
He's marrying Sofia, a **dental hygienist**, next September, and the deposit emptied their savings.
He uses AI **now and then** and waits for senior colleagues before adopting tools.
His edge is **depot knowledge**, and his plan is moving toward robot setup work.
His mood stays **anxious** to **alarmed** when change is fast, and eases with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, landing right after the **wedding** with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: Rules making firms **retrain staff** before cutting them.
A free short course in **robot installation**.
